raw_text:
Transcaval access is a fully percutaneous, transfemoral venous route to the abdominal aorta that was developed to deliver large-bore cardiovascular devices when iliofemoral arterial access is prohibitive. Its clinical relevance has paralleled the expansion of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), which evolved from first-in-human feasibility to established therapy across surgical-risk strata [1–8]. Although contemporary delivery systems are smaller and transfemoral TAVR remains preferred, severe peripheral artery disease, small-caliber vessels, circumferential calcification, tortuosity, prior grafts, or hostile aortoiliac anatomy still create a need for alternative access. Transcaval access is attractive because it preserves the ergonomics and retrograde trajectory of transfemoral TAVR while avoiding thoracotomy, apical puncture, cervical or axillary arterial manipulation, and surgical conduits [9–14].

The principle is counterintuitive but physiologically sound. A guidewire is advanced from the femoral vein into the inferior vena cava (IVC), directed toward a prepositioned aortic snare, and briefly electrified to cross from the IVC into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta [9,10]. After microcatheter exchange and stiff-wire placement, a large-bore sheath is introduced from the femoral vein through the caval–aortic tract into the aorta, permitting standard retrograde valve delivery. At the end of the procedure, the tract is closed with a nitinol occluder, historically an off-label Amplatzer duct or muscular ventricular septal defect occluder, with balloon tamponade or covered stent bailout immediately available [11–14]. The key hemodynamic concept is that retroperitoneal pressure rises and decompresses aortic bleeding into the adjacent low-pressure IVC, producing an aortocaval shunt rather than free retroperitoneal hemorrhage [9,12].

Computed tomography (CT) planning is central. Operators identify a calcium-free right aortic wall target below the renal arteries and above the aortoiliac bifurcation, ensure no interposed bowel or critical venous structures, confirm sufficient sheath working length from the femoral vein to the aorta, and preselect bailout covered-stent dimensions [11,13]. CT also defines fluoroscopic projection angles and vertebral landmarks, enabling reproducible crossing. Technical refinements include buddy-wire protection during closure, protamine reversal before device deployment, systematic assessment of residual shunt patterns, and readiness for aortic balloon occlusion or stent-graft rescue [12,23]. Adjunctive strategies such as laser-assisted crossing have been described for heavily calcified targets but should remain exceptional and operator dependent [17].

Evidence supporting transcaval TAVR began with preclinical validation, followed by a 19-patient initial human experience in otherwise ineligible patients [9,10]. In that series, access and closure were successful in all cases, no death was attributed to transcaval access, and most residual fistulas closed on follow-up imaging [10]. The pivotal prospective multicenter NHLBI study enrolled 100 high- or prohibitive-risk patients unsuitable for conventional femoral access and poor candidates for transthoracic access; transcaval access succeeded in 99%, device success was high, 30-day survival was 92%, and no patient required emergency open repair of the access site [14]. Bleeding and vascular complications were not negligible, reflecting the extreme-risk population, large sheaths, anticoagulation, and permeable off-label closure devices [14,24]. Importantly, 12-month follow-up showed no late major vascular complications, no device migration or fracture, and near-universal fistula closure among evaluable patients [15].

The main limitation of early transcaval practice was closure. Off-label occluders were not designed for immediate hemostasis, contributing to transfusion, residual shunt, and occasional need for covered stents. A purpose-built transcaval closure device demonstrated favorable early feasibility, with improved usability and no transcaval-related major bleeding or major vascular complications in initial testing, but it has not yet become routine clinical equipment [16]. Thus, contemporary best practice still depends on meticulous CT selection, experienced operators, and immediate bailout capability [23].

Comparative data are observational. Single-center and multicenter analyses suggest that transcaval access can achieve outcomes similar to other extrathoracic alternatives and may compare favorably with transaxillary access for neurologic events, while remaining more complex than standard transfemoral TAVR [18–20]. Meta-analyses have reported high technical success and acceptable short-term mortality, bleeding, vascular complication, and stroke rates, but emphasize small samples, selection bias, heterogeneous closure methods, and absence of randomized trials [21,22]. Standardized endpoint definitions, including VARC-2 and VARC-3, are important because residual shunt, CT-detected hematoma, and access-site bleeding may otherwise be reported inconsistently [24,25].

Transcaval access has broader implications for structural and large-bore cardiovascular intervention. It has enabled valve-in-valve and redo TAVR, TAVR in small or grafted aortas, and large-bore mechanical circulatory support when arterial access is inadequate [26,29,30]. These applications reinforce that transcaval access is not simply an alternative “site,” but a platform that converts venous access into temporary controlled aortic access. Current guidelines prioritize transfemoral TAVR when feasible and recommend heart-team selection of alternative routes, considering anatomy, comorbidity, center expertise, and procedural risk [27,28]. In contemporary practice, transcaval access is best reserved for patients without safe transfemoral arterial access in centers with dedicated CT planning, transcatheter electrosurgery expertise, closure-device familiarity, and covered-stent bailout capability. Its future role will depend on dedicated closure technology, prospective comparative studies against transaxillary and transcarotid access, and integration into minimalist TAVR pathways.
